item.title: [amitseg] Miriam Peretz, an Israel Prize laureate, a national symbol of resilience and hope, the mother of two fallen IDF soldiers
item.description:
Open
Miriam Peretz, an Israel Prize laureate, a national symbol of resilience and hope, the mother of two fallen IDF soldiers, and, as of this week, also the mother of a Knesset member from Yashar!, told her friends this week, in shock, what had happened to her son. Elisaf had published a post supporting a Zionist government—seemingly an entirely uncontroversial position. In response, he was subjected to curses and abuse, as though he had proposed joining a coalition under Ben-Gvir rather than simply expressing his party’s official position.

His life is still easier than Netanyahu’s. At the age of 77, the prime minister finds himself in an unfamiliar position: he is the subject of the coalition negotiations, but not an active party to them. Put simply, his ability to control events is extremely limited.

Usually, Netanyahu always has something to offer: a reserved spot on an electoral list, a position, or an attractive political arrangement. Now, heading a caretaker government, with 46 seats and without the most important mandate of all—which currently rests with Eisenkot—he is trying to gather intelligence about the other side’s plans.

Instead of recruiting defectors from the opposing camp, rumors have been circulating within Likud about defections in the opposite direction. David Bitan’s name has been mentioned with concern (he denies it, of course). Netanyahu has no government to offer the ultra-Orthodox parties, and no positions or political prospects to offer potential defectors.

At the beginning of the week, Netanyahu was convinced that a minority government relying on Arab parties would be brought to a vote before the week was out. Later, all the warning lights began flashing over the possibility of cooperation between Lieberman and the ultra-Orthodox parties.

On the morning of the Knesset’s swearing-in ceremony, following a lengthy late-night conversation with the chairman of United Torah Judaism, a temporary all-clear was sounded.

“If you join the coalition,” Netanyahu told Asher, “they will appoint an attorney general and ten Supreme Court justices. And then even a majority of 70 seats won’t help you. You are furious about the conduct of the judicial system, yet you are about to perpetuate it for the next 30 years.”

Whether related or not, the briefings that subsequently emerged from ultra-Orthodox circles became noticeably tougher.

And so came Netanyahu’s speech at the Knesset’s swearing-in ceremony.

Netanyahu had prepared a relatively conciliatory speech, but somewhere along the short walk from the Prime Minister’s Office to the Chagall Hall, it turned into what it ultimately became.

This was not the first time this had happened this year.

Since retiring, Sara Netanyahu has been spending more and more time at her husband’s workplace. The same is true of the newly elected MK Yaakov Bardugo and Netanyahu’s longtime adviser Natan Eshel. All three favor a hard-line approach, bordering on aggressive.

“Did you see how Miriam Peretz applauded his remarks?” people in Likud said delightedly.

But she is not necessarily their target audience.

Likud’s objective is that, in two or three months, if the Lieberman–ultra-Orthodox alliance is thwarted, members of Knesset from the change bloc will face a choice: either a minority government followed by elections, or a national unity government with Netanyahu serving first in a rotation arrangement.

Eisenkot’s reasoning is that if the country heads immediately to elections, relying on the Arab parties would not constitute a permanent arrangement but merely a temporary episode designed to remove Netanyahu from the Prime Minister’s Office.

To accomplish this, he will need Lieberman, but above all, he will need every member of his own parliamentary faction.

Will MKs who strongly oppose forming a government with Arab parties emerge from Netanyahu’s speech feeling that a unity government deserves a chance? Or will they feel precisely the opposite?

One only had to look at the faces of the party leaders during the traditional group photograph. > >
